Dargun
DAR-goon
n. (the Mecklenburg Cistercian abbey of 1172, dissolved 1552 and rebuilt as a ducal palace)
Slavic Dargun, from a personal name, perhaps Dargon.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Dargun in Mecklenburg was founded in 1172 from Esrum, destroyed in a pagan rising, refounded in 1209, and grew into a landed house with granges across the Tollense valley. At the Reformation the community was dissolved in 1552, and the dukes of Mecklenburg-Gūstrow did not pull the buildings down but converted them: the conventual ranges became a residence, and over the next century a palace grew out of the cloister, with the abbey church kept as a court chapel. The dictionary records Dargun for the commonest fate of a dissolved abbey in the Protestant north, which is not destruction but absorption into a nobleman's estate, and for the question that fate raises. The transfer of monastic wealth to princely hands was defended as reform and was very often simple appetite. Christ allows no third master, “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24), and the apostolic diagnosis names the root exactly, “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10). The Lord's warning is against a reckoning of life by holdings, “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15), and the church at Laodicea shows how invisible such wealth makes its own poverty, “I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing” (Rev 3:17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to secularize as to convert to common use; an appropriation as the act of setting apart for a particular use; mammon as riches, wealth personified; covetousness as an inordinate desire of wealth; and a demesne as a manor-house with the adjoining lands.

expand to see more

SECULARIZE, v.t. To convert from spiritual or ecclesiastical appropriation to secular or common use.

APPROPRIATION, n. The act of setting apart or assigning to a particular use, in exclusion of all other uses.

MAMMON, n. Riches; wealth; or the god of riches.

COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good.

DEMESNE, n. A manor-house, and the land adjacent or near, which the lord keeps in his own hands.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

1Ti 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Luk 12:15 — "And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth."

Rev 3:17 — "Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked:"

Modern Corruption

Mecklenburg Cistercian house of 1172 dissolved in 1552 and rebuilt as a ducal palace around the old cloister.

expand to see more

Dargun was not destroyed; it was moved into. The conventual ranges became a palace and the church became a court chapel, and the dukes who arranged it described the transfer as reformation. Some of it was. A great deal of the northern dissolution was appetite wearing the vocabulary of reform, and the Lord's word on the arrangement admits no middle term, “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).

The corruption to name is not only the princes'. The abbeys had themselves grown rich on the theory that endowments purchase masses, so the wealth was corrupt before it changed hands. Paul locates the trouble in an affection rather than in a sum, “which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith” (1Ti 6:10); Christ forbids the arithmetic that equates life with holdings, “Take heed, and beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15); and Laodicea is the standing example of a church that could not see its own condition, “and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked” (Rev 3:17).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek mamonas (G3126), riches, wealth; Greek philarguria (G5365), love of money; Greek pleonexia (G4124), covetousness; Greek talaiporos (G5005), wretched.

expand to see more

Greek mamonas (G3126) — riches, wealth personified; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon”, Matthew 6:24.

Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money, avarice; “For the love of money is the root of all evil”, 1 Timothy 6:10.

Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, a grasping for more; “Take heed, and beware of covetousness”, Luke 12:15.

Greek huparcho (G5225) — to be, to possess, goods on hand; “the things which he possesseth”, Luke 12:15.

Greek talaiporos (G5005) — wretched, afflicted; “thou art wretched, and miserable”, Revelation 3:17.

Usage

"“Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24) — no third master is on offer."

"“For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — the root is an affection, not a sum."

"“I am rich, and increased with goods” (Rev 3:17) — how invisible such wealth makes its poverty."
